walkthroughs.body_html:
Formulae, Equations & Amounts — a core area of A-Level Chemistry.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Formulae, Equations & Amounts brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Formulae, Equations & Amounts.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which species has the same electron configuration as Ar?
options: Na⁺
Cl⁻
F⁻
Mg²⁺

mcqs.q: Successive ionisation energies of an atom always:
options: Decrease
Stay the same
Increase
Vary randomly

mcqs.q: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across a period?
options: Nuclear charge increases while shielding stays roughly constant, so electrons are held more tightly.
Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Atoms get bigger across a period, making electrons easier to add but harder to remove.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.

mcqs.q: If 50 cm^3 of a 1 mol/dm^3 solution is diluted to 100 cm^3, what is the new concentration?
options: The new concentration is 2 mol/dm^3 because adding water makes the solution stronger.
0.5 mol/dm^3 — the moles stay the same but the volume doubled.
The new concentration is 0.05 mol/dm^3 because you doubled the volume so you halve the concentration once and shift the decimal too.
Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.

mcqs.q: Why do tertiary halogenoalkanes typically react via SN1 rather than SN2?
options: Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN1 because they are more reactive in every way.
The tertiary carbocation intermediate is stabilised by three alkyl groups (positive inductive effect), making the SN1 pathway favourable.
Atoms across a period have more shells, pulling electrons closer.
Tertiary halogenoalkanes react via SN2 because they have more bonds to break.
